title: Runbook: DataNode "Got exception while serving block" - Fix
text:
## Fix
- Steady low rate: no action needed.
- One noisy DataNode: take it out of service (decommission), check disk and network, let HDFS re-replicate its blocks.
- Cluster-wide spike: look for a network event or an overloaded job that killed many readers at once.

title: Runbook: DataNode dead or unresponsive - Symptoms
text:
## Symptoms
- The NameNode marks a DataNode dead after it stops sending heartbeats (about 10 minutes by default).
- Write pipelines that include the node fail (EOF, "Could not read from stream", connection reset).
- Readers get "Got exception while serving block" or retry on another replica.
- A wave of re-replication follows, and PendingReplicationMonitor timeouts may appear if the cluster is busy.

title: Runbook: DataNode dead or unresponsive - Common causes
text:
## Common causes
- The machine crashed or rebooted.
- The disk is full or failing, so the DataNode process stops or hangs.
- Long Java garbage-collection pauses make the DataNode miss heartbeats.
- A network switch or cable problem cuts the node (or a whole rack) off.

title: Runbook: DataNode dead or unresponsive - What to check
text:
## What to check
1. Is the DataNode process running? Check its own log for the last messages before it went quiet.
2. Disk space and disk health (`df -h`, SMART errors in the system log).
3. Network: can the NameNode reach the node? Is a whole rack affected?
4. Under-replicated block count on the NameNode (`hadoop fsck /`).

title: Runbook: DataNode dead or unresponsive - Fix
text:
## Fix
- Restart the DataNode once the disk or network problem is fixed.
- If the hardware is bad, decommission the node so HDFS re-replicates its blocks in a controlled way.
- For GC pauses: give the DataNode more heap or reduce load on that machine.

title: Runbook: "PendingReplicationMonitor timed out block" / under-replicated blocks - Overview
text:
**Log pattern:** `WARN dfs.PendingReplicationBlocks$PendingReplicationMonitor: PendingReplicationMonitor timed out block blk_...`
**Component:** NameNode replication monitor.

title: Runbook: "PendingReplicationMonitor timed out block" / under-replicated blocks - What it means
text:
## What it means
When a block has fewer replicas than its target (usually 3), the NameNode asks a DataNode to copy it to
another DataNode and puts the block on a "pending replication" list. If no DataNode confirms the new
replica in time, the request times out and the block goes back on the under-replicated queue to be retried.

title: Runbook: "PendingReplicationMonitor timed out block" / under-replicated blocks - Why it happens
text:
## Why it happens
- The source or target DataNode died or is overloaded.
- The network between racks is saturated (e.g. many blocks re-replicating after a node failure).
- The source replica is corrupt, so the copy keeps failing.

title: Runbook: "PendingReplicationMonitor timed out block" / under-replicated blocks - Why it matters
text:
## Why it matters
Under-replicated blocks are at risk: if the remaining replicas are lost too, the data is gone.
Repeated timeouts for the same block are a sign that something is stuck.

title: Runbook: "PendingReplicationMonitor timed out block" / under-replicated blocks - What to check
text:
## What to check
1. Run `hadoop fsck / -blocks -locations` and look for under-replicated or missing blocks.
2. Check whether a DataNode recently went dead (stopped sending heartbeats).
3. Check whether the same block times out repeatedly.

title: Runbook: "PendingReplicationMonitor timed out block" / under-replicated blocks - Fix
text:
## Fix
- Bring the dead DataNode back, or let re-replication finish.
- If re-replication is overloading the network, limit it (fewer concurrent replication streams per node).
- If a replica is corrupt, delete it so HDFS copies from a healthy replica.

title: Runbook: "Redundant addStoredBlock request received" - Overview
text:
**Log pattern:** `WARN dfs.FSNamesystem: BLOCK* NameSystem.addStoredBlock: Redundant addStoredBlock request received for blk_... on <datanode> size <n>`
**Component:** NameNode (FSNamesystem, block management).

title: Runbook: "Redundant addStoredBlock request received" - What it means
text:
## What it means
A DataNode reported to the NameNode that it stores a block replica, but the NameNode already had that
replica recorded for that DataNode. The second report is "redundant" and is ignored.

title: Runbook: "Redundant addStoredBlock request received" - Why it happens
text:
## Why it happens
- A DataNode re-sent its block report after a timeout or a short network hiccup.
- A DataNode restarted and sent a full block report while the NameNode still remembered it.
- Retries during a slow or failed write pipeline.

title: Runbook: "Redundant addStoredBlock request received" - Is it serious?
text:
## Is it serious?
Usually harmless bookkeeping noise. Many of them at once can mean a DataNode is flapping
(repeatedly disconnecting and reconnecting), or the NameNode is too slow to answer heartbeats.

title: Runbook: "Redundant addStoredBlock request received" - What to check
text:
## What to check
1. Count them per DataNode; one node with many reports may be flapping.
2. Check the NameNode for long garbage-collection pauses or high load around that time.
3. Look for nearby write failures for the same blocks.

title: Runbook: "Redundant addStoredBlock request received" - Fix
text:
## Fix
- Flapping DataNode: check its network link and restart it if needed.
- Overloaded NameNode: give it more heap, or reduce how often DataNodes send full block reports.

title: Runbook: block write pipeline failures - Overview
text:
**Log patterns:**
- `dfs.DataNode$DataXceiver: writeBlock blk_... received exception java.io.IOException: Could not read from stream`
- `writeBlock ... received exception java.io.EOFException` / `java.net.SocketTimeoutException` / `Connection reset by peer`
- `dfs.DataNode$BlockReceiver: Exception in receiveBlock for block blk_...`
- `dfs.DataNode$PacketResponder: PacketResponder ... Exception` or `... Interrupted.`

**Component:** DataNode write path. These lines are logged at INFO level, so counting WARN/ERROR lines misses them.

title: Runbook: block write pipeline failures - What it means
text:
## What it means
HDFS writes a block through a *pipeline* of DataNodes (usually 3 replicas): client -> DN1 -> DN2 -> DN3.
Each DataNode receives packets (BlockReceiver) and passes acknowledgements back (PacketResponder).
If any link in the chain breaks — a node crashes, a disk stalls, the network drops, or the writer dies —
the nodes downstream see "Could not read from stream" or EOF, and the PacketResponder is interrupted.

title: Runbook: block write pipeline failures - Why it matters
text:
## Why it matters
These failures are strongly linked to blocks labelled **anomalous**: the block may end up with fewer
replicas than intended, or a partial replica that has to be cleaned up later.

title: Runbook: block write pipeline failures - What to check
text:
## What to check
1. Find windows where anomalous blocks spike, and see whether write exceptions rise at the same time.
2. Find which DataNode appears in most of the failing pipelines — it is often the broken link.
3. SocketTimeoutException points to a slow or overloaded node; Connection reset points to a crash or network drop.
4. Check that affected blocks were later re-replicated (look for replication requests from the NameNode).

title: Runbook: block write pipeline failures - Fix
text:
## Fix
- Restart or decommission the faulty DataNode.
- For timeouts under heavy load: reduce concurrent writers, or raise the DataNode transfer thread limit and socket timeouts.
- Run `hadoop fsck /` to list under-replicated or corrupt blocks after the incident.
